No Limbs No Limits/Journeyman Special

By: Amalia Christoforou | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Joanne O'Riordan was born with total Amelia - meaning she has no limbs at all. But this has not stopped her from living a most remarkable life.

Summary:
SOURCE: Journeyman
Producer: Steven O'Riordan

"I was born without limbs, but my motto in life is no limbs, no limit" – Joanne O’Riordan

18-year-old Joanne O'Riordan has no arms or legs. One of only seven people in the world to have been born with a condition called Total Amelia, this young woman’s awe-inspiring life has brought her international acclaim. Remarkable footage shows the challenges she has faced since birth and tells of the extent to which ground-breaking technology has replaced her missing limbs. Now, going one step further, she travels from her home in Ireland to the United Nations in New York to issue the ultimate challenge to top influential women in technology – one that will see her independence soar.

No Limbs No Limits

"I was born without limbs, but my motto in life is no limbs, no limit" – Joanne O’Riordan

18-year-old Joanne O'Riordan has no arms or legs. One of only seven people in the world to have been born with a condition called Total Amelia, this young woman’s awe-inspiring life has brought her international acclaim. Remarkable footage shows the challenges she has faced since birth and tells of the extent to which ground-breaking technology has replaced her missing limbs. Now, going one step further, she travels from her home in Ireland to the United Nations in New York to issue the ultimate challenge to top influential women in technology – one that will see her independence soar.
Producer: Steven O'Riordan

**Line-ups are subject to change. Find updates on www.facebook.com/carteblanchetv or twitter.com/carteblanchetv. Scripts and stories can be viewed at www.carteblanche.co.za.
(Images available on request)



Script:


NARRATOR: I want to tell you a story A story about an extraordinary girl Who was born with the most unimaginable disability This girl is so special. There are only 6 others like her, living in the world Joanne was born on the 24th of April 1996 With a medical condition known as... Total Amelia This means, she was born without limbs

NARRATOR: Growing up in a family with 3 older brothers and 1 older sister Joanne was simply adored they have all come together to help her achieve what others would deem impossible This is a tale of honesty, truth, dignity, and bravery It is the story of Irish born Joanne O'Riordan

My name is Joanne O'Riordan and firstly I'd like to thank all those at the UN and the people from the International Telecommunication Union for this amazing and unique opportunity to speak in front of you today Being invited to New York is simply unbelievable As you can see I was born without my limbs, but my motto in life is no limbs, no limits
APPLAUSE
The disability I have is known as Total Amelia and it is one of the world's rarest conditions I believe there are only 7 people living in the world with this physical form And furthermore, there is no medical explanation as to why I was born this way However, my family and I have never allowed it to hold me back From an early age, I have always relied on the use of technology to help advance my abilities My parents have told me that when I was 1 I first began to explore the use of technology with our old computer I figured out how to use the software by simply moving my hand and chin at a faster speed. Today I can type 36 words a minute And for someone with no limbs, I think that's an incredible achievement in itself
APPLAUSE
I also do not look at the word impossible and see it as impossible I look at that word and my life and say I'm possible
APPLAUSE
JOANNE’S MUM: When I knew I was expecting Joanne, pregnant with Joanne, I...I wouldn't be a person for going to the doctors, I never went to the doctors when I was having Gillian and the 3 boys and with Joanne it was the same and in February I thought I'll have to go to the doctors. So I went and um, and I remember saying to the doctor you know, was I maybe on the small side? and he was saying 'No, you're fine, you're grand' and I was saying yeah I suppose I am because it's 8 years since I had a baby and you'd be after forgetting and anyway I'd never really been big with any of the other 4 so why should Joanne be any different?
So, erm... I got the appointment in for March We went up and I went in, on my own and the scan was done And Maire, the woman who did the scan, She said to me, do you know, would I mind... if she brought in the doctor to do the scan as well and then I thought, there's something wrong here, I know there's something wrong But I suppose, what I was to be told I could never have imagined. So erm, the doctor came in and he did the scan and the next thing he just told me that Joanne would be born as she was and I was just, lying there, and...
SOBBING
Joanne was going to be born without her limbs And, my first reaction was like, how dare you talk to me like that about our baby but that was my way of coping pretending to myself, what would the doctors know, after all this was our baby
PIANO PLAYS
JOANNE’S DAD: Just imagine, somebody born without limbs Just take it into your head, to see what, what the person looks like And then, one day I was going over to the garage over to go out to run an errand And Gillian was in the car with me, sitting up in the front seat of the car and she was sitting up in the front seat of the car and she had her legs under her bum and she had her hands behind her back and when I looked over to the passenger side I could just see Gillian without actually any limbs and it was fine Just then it struck me the way Joanne would actually look like And, once I got that into my head how Joanne would look, I was fine with it

JOANNE’S DAD: Yeah JOANNE'S JOANNE’S MUM: And I thought... that's nice because the sun was shining down there and I always wanted the sun shining on our baby. and he walked over to the corner of the room and he washed his hands

JOANNE: All my young life I've struggled and overcome barriers I've surprised doctors, nurses, strangers, friends and even my own family by what I've achieved I'm very lucky that I have the support of my family. They have done everything in their power to ensure that I would not lose out on my education and technology was the key in helping me A system was set which allows my school books to be put onto a CD This in turn enables me to do all my work through a computer Nobody in Ireland has avail of this technology And I was extremely lucky to have a woman by the name of Christine O'Mahony Helping me to make this process much easier It took months to get the format right, but when she did, my life ultimately changed I now discovered that with one flick of my hand I was able to do all the things my other friends were doing with their fingers. I was able to be as good as them if not better. And only the other day I told my mother that technology is the limb I never had.
APPLAUSE
It is fair to say that I have been given the opportunities to grow, learn and adapt my lifestyle in a way that helps me, but I also know there are children and adults out there all over the world who do not have the same chances in life as I do. I'm asking the Girls in Technology who are here today and who are the leading women within their field to start doing what I do, in my life, Think outside the box .
APPLAUSE
Think of ways and means that you can make technology more accessible to those who really need it because let's face it, we all know women are better than men at most things so why not technology too?
LAUGHTER AND APPLAUSE
It is my wish and it's my challenge to you and to others out there... to build me a robot. Yes, that's right a robot! It sounds almost insane but as a child and even today I've always wanted and would love to have a robot. The main thing the robot would be doing is picking up the objects I drop such as a pen, knife, fork, and or my phone. This robot would become my hands and legs. So for example, if I was in the sitting room and I needed something from the kitchen, I would love for that robot to get me what I needed. I mean to be fair when you re lazy and sitting down most of you use a remote control because you re too lazy to get up and manually switch the TV over
LAUGHTER AND APPLAUSE
and trust me that is lazy. So why can't I have a robot? Call it crazy, call it insane, call it what you like but the challenges I face everyday get bigger and far greater to overcome. I know I can overcome these challenges but I need your help. I can't rely on my parents, my brothers, sister and others all my life. Can I? Certainly not and I don't want to! I want to live an independent life just like you. I don't want to live in the shadow of others because I want to make my own journey in life and I know if I'm given that chance I can and will succeed

NARRATOR: Joanne's next trip was to the UK Here she would meet a girl who was also born with Total Amelia. Joanne had met her many years previously and felt it was now time to reconnect with someone who understood her, in a way no one else ever could

JOANNE: I dunno why we keep saying girl, she's like 29. She's typically a woman now Just saying...
STEVEN O'RIORDAN: And how do you find living in the house on your own, independently?
TINA: Amazing. Brilliant. I love being able to do what I wanna do, when I wanna do it. Yeah. I couldn't live at home. I dunno, I couldn't rely on my dad to... take me everywhere and... it's not fair on him Cause I can just get on a train and go wherever I want.

STEVEN O'RIORDAN: Why did you issue a challenge when you were at the United Nations in New York, to build you a robot? Why a robot?
JOANNE: I just think a robot... because I'm so obsessed with technology and, I think, really, when you're at the UN you know, the only reason that was done at the UN was because there were 200 of the smartest people there so you're never gonna have all of them in a room together again and you're probably never gonna get invited to the UN again so I felt that was the right place and the right time to issue that challenge And thankfully they didn t laugh, or LOL or whatever, because they're half crazy as well so they probably liked that whole challenge And assistive living with technology is kind of obviously the way forward in the future so I suppose they enjoyed the whole challenge as well

JOANNE: Urm, obviously picking up stuff and maybe opening doors and getting drinks or setting up a plate, or getting food and stuff like that It's really all, just simple stuff once I'm given the stuff then I can work away with it. Like that's all that has to be done. The stuff needs to get to me first. That's kinda the main problem
TRANQUIL MUSIC
JOANNE: I want a life where I can at least live in my own house And not depend on family members all the time because that's just really annoying for everyone Like it's really frustrating when I'm on my computer and say I drop my pen And say Mum's outside and I have to call her in all the way from the yard or wherever, to come in just to pick up one thing You always feel a bit kind of mean because, you know because whenever they're trying to do something and you call them away they kinda then get moody with you because they were in the middle of doing something important like gardening, or dad was out working or something My parents have this thing in their head, where they can't go out unless they have someone here with me That kinda annoys me because I'm like I can manage for an hour by myself, don't worry about me If the robot comes in, maybe for them it would take away that worry of - Oh Joanne's by herself or whatever I want them to be able to go out without me and I want to be able go out without them

JOANNE: We went over and met Tina And I saw her with her carer and she was saying how she gets 24 hour care I saw her being so independent and that reminded me that I could be exactly the same as her So when you see her doing it, you realise it's already been done so why can't you do it
MUSIC

ENGINEER: Our ultimate goal is to have a robot that can work with you and work for you in your house It's quite human-like. So you've got the upper body like your torso, the thigh, the shin, the arm and the head The main difference is instead of having feet we've got wheels Legs are the most human-like but for general moving around on flat surfaces, wheels are much better for us
ENGINEER 2: Well what I've been working on is the balance of the robot So you saw already that the robot has a lot of moving parts and we need to know where all those parts are and what angle they are So it can stay standing up without falling over or crashing into things This is an early prototype that we built to test our understanding of the sensors. So it balances by itself
JOANNE: This fascinates me
ENGINEER 2: Fundamentally, this robot needs to be able to go where you go So its not just a case of having it in your house and then when you leave the house, it's rooted there It has to be able to come with you to college, it has to be able to go to the shops It has to be able to do all that kind of stuff We heard you had an iPad and an iPhone And this is how we decided we were going to work with it It will connect with the robot wirelessly And you'll have this control there's a couple of buttons there and each has its own command
ENGINEER 3: I'm developing an arm that will be able to pick up different objects that you need picked up during your day The robot will bend over and it'll have to reach down in order to reach the different objects So what we had to do is, we built an arm that can extend itself This is a very early prototype But you can see, it's made of plastic so it’s very lightweight So that keeps the weight down, of the overall machine
NARRATOR: As Joanne begins to forge a new pathway in life, she allows us to see the endless possibilities of what one can achieve resilience and sheer determination have brought her to this place Because Joanne views the world through a different lens, she asks the ultimate question ...What is true independence?

Summary: SOURCE: Journeyman Producer: Steven O'Riordan "I was born without limbs, but my motto in life is no limbs, no limit" – Joanne O’Riordan 18-year-old Joanne O'Riordan has no arms or legs. One of only seven people in the world to have been born with a condition called Total Amelia, this young woman’s awe-inspiring life has brought her international acclaim. Remarkable footage shows the challenges she has faced since birth and tells of the extent to which ground-breaking technology has replaced her missing limbs. Now, going one step further, she travels from her home in Ireland to the United Nations in New York to issue the ultimate challenge to top influential women in technology – one that will see her independence soar. One of only seven people in the world to have been born with a condition called Total Amelia, this young woman’s awe-inspiring life has brought her international acclaim. Remarkable footage shows the challenges she has faced since birth and tells of the extent to which ground-breaking technology has replaced her missing limbs. Now, going one step further, she travels from her home in Ireland to the United Nations in New York to issue the ultimate challenge to top influential women in technology – one that will see her independence soar. Producer: Steven O'Riordan **Line-ups are subject to change. Find updates on www.facebook.com/carteblanchetv or twitter.com/carteblanchetv. Scripts and stories can be viewed at www.carteblanche.co.za. (Images available on request) Script: NARRATOR: I want to tell you a story A story about an extraordinary girl Who was born with the most unimaginable disability This girl is so special. There are only 6 others like her, living in the world Joanne was born on the 24th of April 1996 With a medical condition known as... Total Amelia This means, she was born without limbs PIANO PLAYS NARRATOR: Growing up in a family with 3 older brothers and 1 older sister Joanne was simply adored they have all come together to help her achieve what others would deem impossible This is a tale of honesty, truth, dignity, and bravery It is the story of Irish born Joanne O'Riordan {\an8}MUSIC TRAFFIC CHATTER DOREEN BOGAN MARTIN: Today, we are celebrating Girls and ICT Day and we have a special event here in New York (Doreen Bogdan Martin - Chief Strategic Planning, ITU) focusing on information communication technologies and what it can do for girls KNOCKING JOANNE: Close doors in space JOANNE’S DAD: Good sleep? JOANNE: Yeah, but you snore JOANNE: I did not snore! JOANNE'S DAD: Yes you did JOANNE: But after I told you to shut up, I slept JOANNE'S MUM: Can I spray your clothes? COUGHS Steven O'Riordan: You should give us a run through of your speech now JOANNE: Why? STEVEN O'RIORDAN: Just, you know, warm us all up JOANNE: Ladies and gentlemen, boys and girls Be prepared for the technology speech, by Joanne O'Riordan JOANNE: Ah the dog is so cute APPLAUSE JOANNE: Good afternoon everyone....Yay My name is Joanne O'Riordan and firstly I'd like to thank all those at the UN and the people from the International Telecommunication Union for this amazing and unique opportunity to speak in front of you today Being invited to New York is simply unbelievable As you can see I was born without my limbs, but my motto in life is no limbs, no limits APPLAUSE The disability I have is known as Total Amelia and it is one of the world's rarest conditions I believe there are only 7 people living in the world with this physical form And furthermore, there is no medical explanation as to why I was born this way However, my family and I have never allowed it to hold me back From an early age, I have always relied on the use of technology to help advance my abilities My parents have told me that when I was 1 I first began to explore the use of technology with our old computer I figured out how to use the software by simply moving my hand and chin at a faster speed. Today I can type 36 words a minute And for someone with no limbs, I think that's an incredible achievement in itself APPLAUSE I also do not look at the word impossible and see it as impossible I look at that word and my life and say I'm possible APPLAUSE JOANNE’S MUM: When I knew I was expecting Joanne, pregnant with Joanne, I...I wouldn't be a person for going to the doctors, I never went to the doctors when I was having Gillian and the 3 boys and with Joanne it was the same and in February I thought I'll have to go to the doctors. So I went and um, and I remember saying to the doctor you know, was I maybe on the small side? and he was saying 'No, you're fine, you're grand' and I was saying yeah I suppose I am because it's 8 years since I had a baby and you'd be after forgetting and anyway I'd never really been big with any of the other 4 so why should Joanne be any different? So, erm... I got the appointment in for March We went up and I went in, on my own and the scan was done And Maire, the woman who did the scan, She said to me, do you know, would I mind... if she brought in the doctor to do the scan as well and then I thought, there's something wrong here, I know there's something wrong But I suppose, what I was to be told I could never have imagined. So erm, the doctor came in and he did the scan and the next thing he just told me that Joanne would be born as she was and I was just, lying there, and... SOBBING Joanne was going to be born without her limbs And, my first reaction was like, how dare you talk to me like that about our baby but that was my way of coping pretending to myself, what would the doctors know, after all this was our baby PIANO PLAYS JOANNE’S DAD: Just imagine, somebody born without limbs Just take it into your head, to see what, what the person looks like And then, one day I was going over to the garage over to go out to run an errand And Gillian was in the car with me, sitting up in the front seat of the car and she was sitting up in the front seat of the car and she had her legs under her bum and she had her hands behind her back and when I looked over to the passenger side I could just see Gillian without actually any limbs and it was fine Just then it struck me the way Joanne would actually look like And, once I got that into my head how Joanne would look, I was fine with it MUSIC PLAYS Mum (off camera): Get your bottle Mum (off camera): Good girl! Steven: Did the doctors then have everything in place for Joanne or was there some sort of a plan as to what was gonna happen with Joanne JOANNE’S DAD: No, they had nothingthey hadn't a clue they had never experienced a child born missing their 4 limbs they also had said that the percentage... They also had said that the percentage of the chances of Joanne surviving were very slim So as far as the fellas there were concerned, they felt they didn't have to put anything in place JOANNE’S MUM: They had us convinced so much, that we actually bought a grave for Joanne. We went, I remember going to the graveyard on Easter Sunday and we picked out, we picked out the grave for Joanne and the reason we picked the grave that we picked, was because the sun was shining there JOANNE’S DAD: Yeah JOANNE'S JOANNE’S MUM: And I thought... that's nice because the sun was shining down there and I always wanted the sun shining on our baby. And erm, they told me to come in the following Tuesday, the 23rd of April and that Joanne would be born on the Wednesday by caesarean section Then Joanne was born, at quarter past 9. AD BREAK 1 Segment 1: 08:20 MUSIC PLAYS JOANNE’S DAD: Just kinda the first look after we were talking about how Joanne was born the next thing that popped into my head was the first look What I mean by the first look was, when I looked at Joanne, when I saw Joanne, I thought that... That was the next step, to me, in my part of it and I went into the neonatal and without even being told where to go. I went straight over to this cot and she was wrapped up like you know the child that’s inside there, I wouldn't even know she had been missing her limbs And I just looked down at her and do you know what, she was like a little angel lying there and we bonded the minute we met. And then Sometime during the day the nurse said to me they were bringing Joanne to the room, to me because she didn't have to be above in neonatal. That she was fine, she was grand. And I remember picking Joanne up and I let her in the middle of the bed and I just stood back and I looked over And I looked at Joanne and all I thought was what will you ever do? Not in a bad way. But I just couldn't see, like she was missing limbs, I had never seen someone missing... a hand, one hand or one leg never mind missing all four limbs Baby JOANNE: If you're happy and you know it clap your hands. If you're happy and you know it and you really wanna show it If you're happy and you know it clap your hands. Boom, boom. JOANNE SINGING JOANNE: Stamp your feet! JOANNE’S MUM: I did. You hear me. JOANNE: Help me, go get a drink JOANNE’S MUM: I will help you to drink when you walk As soon as you go down to Daddy now, I'll get you a drink of water I sit down then and you must walk down to me to get it. Is that fair now? Yep. I walk down to Daddy like this JOANNE: Dad JOANNE'S DAD: Yes? JOANNE: You sit down! Sit down! Mum, you give me the cup JOANNE'S DAD: Go over and get the cup JOANNE: I can't! I can't reach it, I'll fall down! JOANNE'S DAD: Go on, I'll push it in a small bit LAUGHS JOANNE’S MUM: And I remember saying to the doctor that someone had said to us that Joanne might be able to be fitted with a prosthetic hand on her left hand side because of the piece that she had and I remember him saying to us, who told you that? And we said, somebody told us, a doctor told us and he goes Well I'm the doctor, you listen to me JOANNE'S MUM:, I can still see him like, he just stood over he and he looked at her And then he told me that, do you know when you get a doll for Christmas, and I goes right... and do you know, he told me, when one hand falls off, the other hand falls off, then the legs fall off. What do you do with the doll? And I said, I don t know, what do you do with the doll? Well you put it into a cupboard, whatever you wanted to do with it Put it away He was telling us, that when we actually got tired of Joanne that we could actually put Joanne into a home He was telling us without telling us, do you know what I mean? The tears. I'll never forget it the longest I live I cried, cried and cried never touched Joanne and he walked over to the corner of the room and he washed his hands JOANNE'S MUM: That man, I said, is not going to...It was he actually who put the drive in us JOANNE'S DAD: Well, he put the drive in us JOANNE'S MUM: He was cruel and horrible and what have you, But we thought, we'll prove him wrong We'll get Joanne up and going... and we'll prove that man wrong. MUSIC PLAYS (Voice, off camera) Very good! TV PRESENTER KENNY (off camera): There is no other baby like her in Ireland nor has there ever been. Across the world children like her are exceptionally rare. Will you give a very warm welcome please to Joe and Anna O'Riordan and baby Joanne. {\an8}APPLAUSE KENNY: What's ahead of you clearly... I mean, you re not well resourced, you don t have a lot of money Both parents: No. K: And you've decided to try and raise funds Both: That's right KENNY: You've got an ambitious target NARRATOR: That appearance, on the Kenny Live Show provoked a public reaction never seen before A worldwide campaign was launched and a staggering 800,000 pounds was donated to the Joanne O'Riordan fund TRIUMPHANT MUSIC PLAYS The generosity and kindness of strangers, allowed Joanne's family to provide her with a better standard of living and a new world of possibilities. People from every walk of life did what they could to support this special little girl Voice (off camera) Super duper! NARRATOR: As she grew, friendships blossomed and her school environment allowed her to excel beyond expectation It was now time for Joanne to find her own distinctive voice. {\an8}CHATTER/LAUGHTER JOANNE: So Enda Kenny will be here in a few minutes He needs to shake hands with a few of the locals and they will get the inside scoop out of Enda Kenny Voice (off camera): Right, he's coming out JOANNE: We've just heard that Enda Kelly will be arriving in 2 minutes Count 'em... 2... 1.59... 1.58... and so on NEWS REPORTER: Joanne featured extensively in the media last December when the government was forced to reverse the cut to the disability allowance in the budget after footage was released of Taoiseach Enda Kelly promising her, that the allowance wouldn't be touched. ENDA KELLY: Before the Christmas, in our budget presentation we're not taking any money off people with disability. we want that protected. Is that ok Joanne? JOANNE: Yeah. RADIO PRESENTER: Regular listeners to C103 are well aware of Joanne O'Riordan She's become not just a local hero to us, but a national hero to many TV Presenter (The Late Late show): Would you welcome please, Joanne O'Riordan TV PRESENTER (The Late Late show): Would you welcome please, Joanne O'Riordan APPLAUSE NARRATOR: As Joanne evoked change in government policy,she now became a beacon of light for all those living in Ireland. PRESENTER (Late Late show): You hear that cheer in the crowd, it was because, you took them on and you won APPLAUSE NARRATOR: It was at this point, Joanne received an invitation to address the United AD BREAK 2 Segment 2 - 07:33 JOANNE’S MUM: Do you want to wear your glasses? JOANNE: Yes. JOANNE: Are you seriously wearing socks and sandals? ...Oh my god! Oh god... They all wear socks and sandals ELECTRIC TOOTHBRUSH BUZZING NEWS PROGRAMME THEME A 15 year old County Cork school girl who was born without limbs will address the United Nations Council in New York on how she's used technology to improve her quality of life Joanne O'Riordan is one of the few people worldwide living with Total Amelia But she says she doesn't regard her condition as a disability DOORS SLAM {\an8}AIRPORT ANNOUNCEMENT JOANNE: Thanks very much! Yes, we're all good. JOANNE: Thanks very much. Bye... Bye NARRATOR: And so, as Joanne jetted off to the land of opportunity A worldwide audience waited, waited with anticipation, waited to hear what this young Irish girl had to offer GUITAR PLAYS IN BACKGROUND NARRATOR: Having touched down in New York Joanne received an invitation to meet with Grammy award-winner and songwriter Julie Gold Julie is best known for the renowned classic From a Distance And having seen a preview copy of Joanne's speech Julie decided to pen a song inspired by her life story JULIE GOLD: I'm so excited! {\an8}TAPPING FEET Steven: Joanne, this way. JOANNE: You said right. H: Straight on and then right JG: I hear a voice, I hear your voice! I've beenstudying it...Welcome to New York! JOANNE: Thank you very much JG: Welcome to... our humble abode Tell me what your first impression was, could you see the skyline when you came in? JOANNE: Yeah we could see everything and, like, I love seeing all the tall buildings JG: This is unbelievable It's the city where everybody comes to fulfill their dreams, so the energy is so high...Wait till you see what I did with our song JOANNE: Our song JG: Because I read your UN speech and it... it inspired something...That speech is fantastic. JOANNE: Thank you very much JG: Are you nervous? JOANNE: Um, more excited than nervous I think JG: Yeah... That's well put JG: You know I was very taken by one of your lines, which I thought was so magnificent was you know, that when you hear the word impossible... JOANNE: Oh, I'm possible JG: Yeah, it's brilliant. And now I've added this PLAYING PIANO JG: Nothing is impossible. I'm possible. I'm possible. Nothing is impossible. I'm possible. La la la, la, la Hey, have you heard? My heart is a bird It takes me as far as I can dream Over the crowds, over the clouds There aren't limits Nothing is impossible. I'm possible. I'm possible. Nothing is impossible. I'm possible, la la la la la la APPLAUSE JOANNE: All my young life I've struggled and overcome barriers I've surprised doctors, nurses, strangers, friends and even my own family by what I've achieved I'm very lucky that I have the support of my family. They have done everything in their power to ensure that I would not lose out on my education and technology was the key in helping me A system was set which allows my school books to be put onto a CD This in turn enables me to do all my work through a computer Nobody in Ireland has avail of this technology And I was extremely lucky to have a woman by the name of Christine O'Mahony Helping me to make this process much easier It took months to get the format right, but when she did, my life ultimately changed I now discovered that with one flick of my hand I was able to do all the things my other friends were doing with their fingers. I was able to be as good as them if not better. And only the other day I told my mother that technology is the limb I never had. APPLAUSE It is fair to say that I have been given the opportunities to grow, learn and adapt my lifestyle in a way that helps me, but I also know there are children and adults out there all over the world who do not have the same chances in life as I do. I'm asking the Girls in Technology who are here today and who are the leading women within their field to start doing what I do, in my life, Think outside the box . APPLAUSE Think of ways and means that you can make technology more accessible to those who really need it because let's face it, we all know women are better than men at most things so why not technology too? LAUGHTER AND APPLAUSE It is my wish and it's my challenge to you and to others out there... to build me a robot. Yes, that's right a robot! It sounds almost insane but as a child and even today I've always wanted and would love to have a robot. The main thing the robot would be doing is picking up the objects I drop such as a pen, knife, fork, and or my phone. This robot would become my hands and legs. So for example, if I was in the sitting room and I needed something from the kitchen, I would love for that robot to get me what I needed. I mean to be fair when you re lazy and sitting down most of you use a remote control because you re too lazy to get up and manually switch the TV over LAUGHTER AND APPLAUSE and trust me that is lazy. So why can't I have a robot? Call it crazy, call it insane, call it what you like but the challenges I face everyday get bigger and far greater to overcome. I know I can overcome these challenges but I need your help. I can't rely on my parents, my brothers, sister and others all my life. Can I? Certainly not and I don't want to! I want to live an independent life just like you. I don't want to live in the shadow of others because I want to make my own journey in life and I know if I'm given that chance I can and will succeed APPLAUSE AND MUSIC NARRATOR: The challenge was set and the message was clear: Build me a robot. THIRD ad break Segment 3 – 08:38 OUTRO LINK Segment 4: INTRO LINK: Having set the technology world alight Joanne arrived home to a flurry of invites to conferences and events all over Ireland. Her voice enabled others, to see beyond their own limitations APPLAUSE AND CHEERING Subsequently, the Irish public nominated Joanne as their Rehab Young Person of the Year MUSIC AND APPLAUSE NARRATOR: Joanne's next trip was to the UK Here she would meet a girl who was also born with Total Amelia. Joanne had met her many years previously and felt it was now time to reconnect with someone who understood her, in a way no one else ever could STEVEN: Where are you going today? JOANNE: We're meeting a girl called Tina JOANNE: I dunno why we keep saying girl, she's like 29. She's typically a woman now Just saying... STEVEN O'RIORDAN: And how do you find living in the house on your own, independently? TINA: Amazing. Brilliant. I love being able to do what I wanna do, when I wanna do it. Yeah. I couldn't live at home. I dunno, I couldn't rely on my dad to... take me everywhere and... it's not fair on him Cause I can just get on a train and go wherever I want. STEVEN O'RIORDAN: So in the morning, like Mum gets Joanne out of bed, does your carer have to...? TINA: Yeah, well I have 24 hour care and they do shift work. So, they live here and sleep here STEVEN O'RIORDAN: And who pays for that? TINA: Uh, direct payments... STEVEN O'RIORDAN: From the government? TINA: Yeah STEVEN O'RIORDAN: Ok. And did you have to fight to get that? TINA: Yeah. It took like... They keep trying to take it off me Like, why do you need 24 hour care? ...um Hmm, I don't know Why do you think? It all comes down to money though doesn't it, in the end that's all they care about TINA: It's just so nice to talk to someone who's like me. It's just mad. JOANNE: I know. It's such a pity we live so far... well not even far away but 'Cause the others live way further TINA: Yeah, like not everyday you get to meet somebody that has the same rare disability JOANNE: There's only 7 of us! TINA: I can't believe that JOANNE: There's only 7 MUSIC PLAYS TINA: All better now JOANNE: You're looking stunning, babes TINA: Let's go for a wee walk JOANNE: Turn Tina, turn! DOOR BANGS TINA: Oh geez! I did that on purpose! JOANNE: I fitted out, I'm slim...Let's go to the beach, beach. Woohoo JOANNE: People are staring. Let's wave... Everyone's like look at that, there's two! STEVEN O'RIORDAN: Just bring me back to the first time that you remember meeting Joanne TINA: I was just like wow. This is a little girl who's exactly the same as me. It's just crazy because I didn't know there was anyone else like me in the world really Well, you don't really think about it at that age but yeah it was really cool Just like s Just like she's gonna grow up and be able to do stuff like I do and stuff -It's cool because I could show her... Well, I could show her parents what she'd be able to do when she was older and stuff STEVEN O'RIORDAN: And you've been adopted right? And so just talk to me about that, or talk about your biological mum and how you became adopted by your adoptive parents TINA: Well, I think when my mum had me I dunno if it was the shock or what but, she didn't think she could cope and, put me up for adoption. I was in the hospital till I was about 5 months old and then my mum and dad, Katie and Chris, came along and wanted to adopt me Well, foster me at first. So I went to live with them when I was 5 months old And then they adopted me when I was 3 They've been like the best parents and made me the most independent I can be I was just like any other ordinary kid, just going out and playing with their friends I think the way my mum and dad have brought me up is like, I am just like anybody else. STEVEN O'RIORDAN: I think, was it last year, your adopted mother passed away? TINA: Yeah, it was really, really hard to lose mum JOANNE: Channing Tatum was so lovely TINA: Channing Tatum, I'd love to meet him DOG HOWLING FOURTH ad break Segment 4 – 07:31 STEVEN O'RIORDAN: Why did you issue a challenge when you were at the United Nations in New York, to build you a robot? Why a robot? JOANNE: I just think a robot... because I'm so obsessed with technology and, I think, really, when you're at the UN you know, the only reason that was done at the UN was because there were 200 of the smartest people there so you're never gonna have all of them in a room together again and you're probably never gonna get invited to the UN again so I felt that was the right place and the right time to issue that challenge And thankfully they didn t laugh, or LOL or whatever, because they're half crazy as well so they probably liked that whole challenge And assistive living with technology is kind of obviously the way forward in the future so I suppose they enjoyed the whole challenge as well STEVEN: And what kind of things would the robot do to assist you in living? JOANNE: Urm, obviously picking up stuff and maybe opening doors and getting drinks or setting up a plate, or getting food and stuff like that It's really all, just simple stuff once I'm given the stuff then I can work away with it. Like that's all that has to be done. The stuff needs to get to me first. That's kinda the main problem TRANQUIL MUSIC JOANNE: I want a life where I can at least live in my own house And not depend on family members all the time because that's just really annoying for everyone Like it's really frustrating when I'm on my computer and say I drop my pen And say Mum's outside and I have to call her in all the way from the yard or wherever, to come in just to pick up one thing You always feel a bit kind of mean because, you know because whenever they're trying to do something and you call them away they kinda then get moody with you because they were in the middle of doing something important like gardening, or dad was out working or something My parents have this thing in their head, where they can't go out unless they have someone here with me That kinda annoys me because I'm like I can manage for an hour by myself, don't worry about me If the robot comes in, maybe for them it would take away that worry of - Oh Joanne's by herself or whatever I want them to be able to go out without me and I want to be able go out without them STEVEN: At 3 o'clock in the morning when you're looking at the world go by and you can't sleep and the pillows annoying you in bed cause you're trying to twist and turn is there anything that makes you go, do you know what I wish I had limbs? JOANNE: I suppose you do but you can't dwell on it for too long because then you get depressed. So, I don't really dwell on it too often And if I do, it's only momentarily, its not gonna last forever. JOANNE: We went over and met Tina And I saw her with her carer and she was saying how she gets 24 hour care I saw her being so independent and that reminded me that I could be exactly the same as her So when you see her doing it, you realise it's already been done so why can't you do it MUSIC ENGINEER: Our ultimate goal is to have a robot that can work with you and work for you in your house It's quite human-like. So you've got the upper body like your torso, the thigh, the shin, the arm and the head The main difference is instead of having feet we've got wheels Legs are the most human-like but for general moving around on flat surfaces, wheels are much better for us ENGINEER 2: Well what I've been working on is the balance of the robot So you saw already that the robot has a lot of moving parts and we need to know where all those parts are and what angle they are So it can stay standing up without falling over or crashing into things This is an early prototype that we built to test our understanding of the sensors. So it balances by itself JOANNE: This fascinates me ENGINEER 2: Fundamentally, this robot needs to be able to go where you go So its not just a case of having it in your house and then when you leave the house, it's rooted there It has to be able to come with you to college, it has to be able to go to the shops It has to be able to do all that kind of stuff We heard you had an iPad and an iPhone And this is how we decided we were going to work with it It will connect with the robot wirelessly And you'll have this control there's a couple of buttons there and each has its own command ENGINEER 3: I'm developing an arm that will be able to pick up different objects that you need picked up during your day The robot will bend over and it'll have to reach down in order to reach the different objects So what we had to do is, we built an arm that can extend itself This is a very early prototype But you can see, it's made of plastic so it’s very lightweight So that keeps the weight down, of the overall machine NARRATOR: As Joanne begins to forge a new pathway in life, she allows us to see the endless possibilities of what one can achieve resilience and sheer determination have brought her to this place Because Joanne views the world through a different lens, she asks the ultimate question ...What is true independence?
